brief.intro: New to this project type? An LNG terminal stores and handles liquefied natural gas at around minus 162°C, which makes it fundamentally a cryogenic process plant: large insulated storage tanks, cryogenic-rated piping and pumps, and — depending on the terminal — either liquefaction trains that cool gas into LNG or regasification trains that warm LNG back into gas for the grid, plus a marine jetty where ships load or unload. The programme is dominated by heavy process piping and pipe-spool fabrication, by the tanks themselves, and above all by fire & gas safety systems, because a cryogenic and highly flammable product demands an unusually safety-heavy commissioning process before any LNG is introduced. Civil works — tank foundations, the marine jetty and berth — are substantial but are enablers to the process systems, not the schedule driver in their own right. Commissioning is staged and deliberately slow: tanks and piping must be dried, inerted and then cooled down gradually before first LNG, and fire & gas / emergency shutdown systems must be proven before that cooldown is allowed to begin.

scope.name: Site & marine civil works
scope.desc: Tank foundations, process-area paving, marine works (jetty/berth), drainage and containment.

scope.name: LNG storage tanks
scope.desc: Full-containment or double-containment cryogenic tanks with insulation and instrumentation.

scope.name: Process piping & pipe-spool fabrication
scope.desc: Cryogenic and process-grade piping, much of it shop-fabricated as spools.

scope.name: Liquefaction / regasification trains
scope.desc: Compressors, heat exchangers, vaporizers and associated rotating and process equipment.

scope.name: Marine jetty & loading arms
scope.desc: Berth structure, LNG loading/unloading arms and the ship interface.

scope.name: Fire & gas safety systems
scope.desc: Fire & gas detection, deluge/foam firefighting and the emergency shutdown (ESD) system.

scope.name: Electrical power
scope.desc: Power distribution for process, utilities and hazardous-area equipment.

scope.name: Instrumentation & control (DCS/SIS)
scope.desc: Process control and safety-instrumented systems across the terminal.

scope.name: Testing & commissioning
scope.desc: Drying, inerting, controlled cooldown, and leak/pressure testing ahead of first LNG.

must_get_right: Fire & gas / ESD safety systems must be fully proven before cooldown or first LNG is allowed — never compress this stage to protect the schedule.
Cryogenic cooldown is a slow, physics-bound process, not a task you can crash — build the real duration into the baseline, not an optimistic guess.
Pipe-spool fabrication (cryogenic and process grade) is typically the long-lead, high-volume critical path — track fabrication and delivery by spool count, not as one lump activity.
The marine jetty and civil works are enablers to the process systems, not the driver — don't let civil 'looking busy' hide slippage in tanks, piping and safety systems.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. Mechanical completion is tracked by system and subsystem, as is standard for process plants, so pre-commissioning can start on completed systems while other systems are still under construction.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Civil and marine works run a standard shift with tidal/weather windows for marine construction; piping and equipment installation move to extended shifts approaching mechanical completion. Once started, drying, inerting and cooldown run on a continuous (24-hour) calendar, since these are physically continuous processes that cannot be stopped and restarted without cost.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: The driving path runs tank/piping long-lead procurement → spool fabrication → tank and piping erection → equipment set → fire & gas/ESD proving → mechanical completion → drying/inerting → controlled cooldown → first LNG. Fire & gas/ESD proving is an explicit gate before cooldown is permitted to begin — cooldown cannot start until the safety system is proven.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: Tank design is frozen early given its fabrication lead time; LNG carrier and berth compatibility is confirmed; there is a single defined point of first-cargo readiness; and no scope change is made to safety-critical systems after issue-for-construction. Any change to these invalidates the baseline dates.

sections.heading: Procurement & long-lead items
sections.body: The schedule is procurement-led. The following are tracked as milestones and drive the network:

rows: Compressors / heat exchangers (liquefaction or regas train)

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Marine works are constrained by tide and weather windows; compressors and heat exchangers require heavy-lift access before the site becomes congested; specialist cryogenic welders and NDT technicians are a shared, constrained resource across spool fabrication; hazardous-area work requires formal permits and gas-freeing before hot work.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Principal risks: cryogenic material and valve lead-time slippage, marine works weather delay, fire & gas/ESD proof-test rework loops, and spool fabrication quality rejects. Schedule contingency is held before the fire & gas/ESD proving gate and before first-LNG cooldown rather than spread thinly across individual systems.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones — mechanical completion, ESD proven, first LNG) and Level 2 (summary by system/train) to the client; controlled at Level 3; expanded to Level 4–5 lookahead per spool/system for the field — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
